abstract.p: The excessive use of antibiotics presents significant risks, as it not only drives the emergence of antibiotic resistance in microbial pathogens but also disrupts the microbial communities essential for maintaining normal human physiological functions. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have garnered increasing attention as a highly promising alternative to antibiotics. The use of computational methods to identify AMPs is becoming increasingly popular, as these approaches can considerably reduce the time and cost involved. In this work, we propose a deep learning-based AMP recognition framework, CG-AMP, aimed at efficiently identifying AMPs. CG-AMP adopts a dual-module architecture, where the first module learns the feature representation space through a pre-trained language model and contrastive learning, while the second module incorporates an enhanced Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to more efficiently extract feature information. This design aims to effectively integrate multimodal features by combining the strengths of both methods, thereby enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of AMP identification. We evaluated CG-AMP on two independent test sets and compared its performance with current state-of-the-art models. The results demonstrated that CG-AMP was a reliable AMP identification tool. Specifically, on the AMPlify and DAMP test sets, CG-AMP achieved accuracies of 0.9497 and 0.9403, F1 scores of 0.9508 and 0.9392, and Matthews correlation coefficients of 0.8994 and 0.8812, respectively, outperforming other existing methods.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The widespread application of antibiotics causes bacteria to develop resistance mechanisms1. Based on a 2019 report by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and Prevention, around 2.8 million cases of infections caused by resistant bacteria arise annually in the United States, leading to more than 35,000 deaths2. In Europe, approximately 33,000 deaths are attributed to resistant bacterial infections each year3. Therefore, given the severe antibiotic resistance issues arising from the overuse of antibiotics and the resulting threat to public health, there is an immediate need to develop novel alternatives to antibiotics4,5. It is worth noting that Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have been described as broad-spectrum antimicrobial or immunomodulatory molecules that can directly target microorganisms, often resulting in cell lysis or regulating the host’s immune system to strengthen defense against microorganisms6. Additionally, they exhibit a faster action rate compared to traditional antibiotics7. After millions of years of evolution, although bacteria have been continuously exposed to AMPs, significant development of resistance has not occurred8. With their broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, fast-acting mechanism, and low resistance risk, AMPs are regarded as ideal candidates for replacing traditional antibiotics in the future9,10.

Screening for new AMPs through wet-lab experiments on a large scale is time-consuming, expensive, and labor-intensive11. Therefore, over the past few decades, machine learning-based approaches have been extensively utilized to accelerate the identification of AMPs and have achieved remarkable results. Initially, Fjell et al.12 used a Hidden Markov Model for the clustering and analysis of AMPs. Later, Randou et al.13 introduced a logistic regression-based method for AMP identification. Subsequently, Veltri et al.14 and Meher et al.15 developed AMP recognition models using Random Forest and Support Vector Machine, respectively, and demonstrated good performance on benchmark datasets. Currently, owing to the powerful sequence representation and automatic feature extraction capabilities of deep learning methods16–18, models based on deep learning are gaining increasing attention in scientific research, particularly in applications within fields such as bioinformatics. Han et al.19 developed an ensemble model called TriStack, which combines deep learning and machine learning methods for AMP identification. Li et al.20 applied an attention mechanism as the backbone network in their model, while Veltri et al.21 adopted Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks as classifiers for AMP recognition. Zhang et al.22 proposed a BERT-based model for AMP identification. The model is first pre-trained on sequence data obtained from the UniProt23 database and then fine-tuned on six different datasets to enhance its performance. Sharma et al.24 compared the performance of eight different models in the task of AMP identification and conducted an in-depth analysis of the impact of various input features and network architectures on model performance. Through systematic experiments and evaluations, they found that the model using word2vec as the input feature and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM)25 as the core framework achieved the best performance. In addition, some models leveraged structural information to learn features. For example, the models developed by Hao et al.26 and Cordoves-Delgado et al.27 combined both sequence and structural features to perform prediction, employing Graph Neural Networks (GNN) as the backbone network. Protein structures encompass all essential information encoded in their sequences. Therefore, in general, structure-based models tend to offer superior performance compared to sequence-based models. However, to maintain high model accuracy, structure-based approaches must rely on accurate protein structures as input28,29. Therefore, utilizing protein sequences for AMP identification remains an urgent and critical research challenge.

Although machine learning and deep learning-based approaches have shown significant progress in AMP identification, traditional sequence-driven models have yet to achieve optimal performance in practical applications and still exhibit certain limitations. For example, recent models such as AMPlify and TriStack have achieved notable results but predominantly rely on conventional handcrafted features and limited feature fusion strategies. In particular, AMPlify uses BiLSTM for feature extraction, which increases computational overhead. Overall, most existing methods face several issues: firstly, most existing methods rely on a limited set of feature descriptors, frequently neglecting critical features with evolutionary information, physicochemical properties, or features extracted through pre-trained models, which impacts the models’ accuracy and generalization ability. Secondly, many existing methods typically employ simple feature fusion strategies or a unified network architecture for feature extraction, neglecting the complementarity and diversity among different features. Finally, although LSTM25 and other recurrent neural networks exhibit significant advantages in modeling sequence context relationships, their large number of parameters may introduce redundant information or increase computational overhead during short peptide feature extraction, thereby affecting the model’s computational efficiency and generalization ability.

Pretraining and contrastive learning are two effective representation learning methods. Pretraining involves leveraging large amounts of unlabeled data to train models within an unsupervised context, with the trained parameters then transferred to downstream tasks for adaptive optimization or feature extraction30. This approach is commonly applied in applications like protein structure and function prediction31,32. Contrastive learning, on the other hand, focuses on constructing a representation space where similar samples are positioned closer together, while samples from different categories are kept apart. This strategy significantly enhances the quality of protein embeddings and has improved model performance in areas like protein-ligand interaction prediction33,34 and protein-DNA interaction prediction35. Furthermore, CNN36,37 serve as a powerful tool for feature extraction, effectively capturing local patterns within sequential data. However, traditional CNNs exhibit limitations in modeling long-range dependencies. To address the limitations of conventional CNN in modeling long-range dependencies, we introduce Gated Convolutional Neural Network (GCNN)38. This method combines the parallelism of convolutional operations with the selectivity of gating mechanisms, thereby enhancing the capacity for feature representation. Moreover, it achieves performance comparable to, or even surpassing, that of LSTM models, while maintaining lower computational cost. GCNN has already shown promising results in tasks such as affinity prediction39.

In this work, we develop a novel dual-module neural network framework, CG-AMP, specifically designed for the identification of AMPs. This framework extracts rich feature representations from different perspectives of AMP sequences, encompassing features obtained through a pre-trained language model, features containing evolutionary information, and features reflecting physicochemical properties. We define the integrated features that combine evolutionary information and physicochemical attributes as multi-dimensional features. To enhance the efficiency of learning these multi-view features, we propose a dual-module strategy. The contrastive learning module integrates a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) encoder and optimizes the pre-trained features through contrastive learning, thereby enhancing their discriminative ability, while the GCNN module employs a GCNN to capture the sequential contextual information of the multidimensional features. ​Each module is responsible for extracting and learning different types of complementary features, which are subsequently integrated through an efficient fusion mechanism, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy of AMP identification. Compared with other integration strategies, the proposed design achieves deep complementarity between semantic and physicochemical features and balances global and local dependency modeling. As a result, it generates peptide representations that are more informative, stable, and generalizable, substantially enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AMP identification.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: We employed two benchmark datasets, AMPlify20 and DAMP21, for model validation and performance evaluation. The AMPlify dataset was compiled by integrating sequence data from multiple authoritative public databases. Its positive sample set was primarily sourced from the Antimicrobial Peptide Database (APD3)40 and the Database of Anuran Defense Peptides (DADP)41. After removing redundant sequences and filtering based on length (excluding peptide sequences longer than 200 residues), a final positive sample set of 4,173 unique and mature AMPs was obtained. The negative sample set was carefully curated from the UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot23 database. First, researchers excluded all sequences containing any of the following 16 keywords associated with antimicrobial activity: antibiotic, antifungal, anti-protist, antimicrobial, histatin, bacteriocin, microbicidal, defense, defensin, antimalarial, antiparasitic, cathelicidin, fungicide, anticancer, antiviral, and antibacterial. Additionally, duplicate entries were removed, and sequences containing any non-standard amino acid residues were filtered out. Ultimately, 4,173 sequences were randomly selected from the remaining 128,445 non-AMP sequences to match the size of the positive sample set. Additionally, the length distribution of the negative sample set was adjusted to match that of the positive sample set. This strategy ensured the balance and reliability of the dataset. The AMPlify dataset was split into a training set and a test set with a 4:1 proportion. The training set was then further divided into a training subset and a validation set in a 7:1 ratio (as shown in Table 1). The DAMP database was developed by Veltri et al. By applying strict sequence filtering criteria with a sequence similarity threshold of 40%, the researchers constructed a balanced dataset consisting of 3,556 samples (1,778 AMPs and 1,778 non-AMPs). This dataset was subsequently divided into training, validation, and test sets in a 2:1:2 ratio, resulting in 1,424, 708, and 1,424 samples, respectively (as shown in Table 1).

sec.title: Model architecture
sec.p: In this study, we propose a computational framework named CG-AMP, designed for the prediction and identification of AMPs. The construction of CG-AMP involves four core steps: data preparation, input feature encoding, neural network architecture design, and model evaluation. First, during the data preparation phase, we utilize benchmark datasets from AMPlify and DAMP to ensure the reliability of data used for model training and validation. Second, to transform AMP sequence information into a format suitable for neural network processing, we employ a combination of a pre-trained language model, one-hot encoding, BLOSUM62 encoding, and Z-scale encoding to convert sequences into numerical matrices, thereby completing the representation of input features. Third, we design a dual-module feature extraction framework to separately process ESM-2 embeddings and multi-dimensional handcrafted features (BLOSUM62, Z-scale, and one-hot encoding). Each feature type is independently encoded via contrastive learning and gated convolutional neural network (GCNN) modules to capture semantic and physicochemical information. We evaluate several feature fusion strategies, including simple concatenation, linear fusion, and attention-based fusion, and found that linear fusion achieves the best balance between model performance and complexity. The selected features are biologically complementary: ESM-2 embeddings capture contextual and evolutionary semantics, while handcrafted features provide residue-level physicochemical information, enabling a rich and multi-perspective representation of peptide sequences. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive performance evaluation of CG-AMP using two test datasets to assess the accuracy and reliability of its predictive capability. The results indicate that, while maintaining the same hyperparameter settings (optimized on the AMPlify dataset), CG-AMP not only achieves outstanding performance across multiple benchmark datasets but also demonstrates strong generalization capability. In conclusion, CG-AMP integrates contrastive learning with a GCNN within a dual-module architecture to achieve accurate and robust AMP prediction. By effectively capturing and fusing multiple complementary feature representations, the proposed framework demonstrates clear methodological advancements and consistent performance improvements over existing approaches, providing new insights and valuable guidance for AMP-related research. sec.title: Comparison with other methods
sec.p: To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of the CG-AMP framework, we conducted experimental assessments and comparative analyses on both the AMPlify and DAMP datasets. By comparing the prediction results obtained from our model on the test set with those from current.

mainstream models (including TriStack, AMPlify, AMPscanner Vr2 (re-trained)21, PepNet47, and CG-AMP-MC, a strong baseline model using only pooled ESM-2 embeddings processed through an MLP encoder for prediction), we performed an in-depth analysis. Based on the experimental results in Tables 4 and 5, the CG-AMP model exhibits outstanding performance in classification accuracy and other key evaluation metrics, significantly outperforming existing comparison models. On the AMPlify dataset, CG-AMP achieved the best results across five evaluation metrics (Accuracy, F1-score, Recall, Precision, and MCC), demonstrating exceptional overall predictive capability. In terms of accuracy and MCC, CG-AMP reached 0.9497 and 0.8994, respectively, which are significantly higher than TriStack, with values of 0.9215 and 0.8429, showing improvements of approximately 2.8% and 5.7%. It is noteworthy that, compared with CG-AMP-MC (Accuracy 0.9275, MCC 0.8549), the dual-module design of CG-AMP improves Accuracy and MCC by approximately 2.2% and 4.5%, respectively, indicating that the performance gain brought by the dual-module architecture exceeds what can be achieved by relying solely on a powerful pre-trained model. On the DAMP dataset, due to the relatively small size of the training samples, the models participating in the experiment exhibited overall lower performance compared to their results on the AMPlify dataset. Despite this, CG-AMP still outperforms others in accuracy (0.9403) and MCC (0.8812), showing improvements of approximately 3.2% and 6.5%, respectively, over TriStack.

Furthermore, CG-AMP also demonstrates the best performance in Precision, F1-score, and Recall, showcasing excellent classification stability and strong cross-dataset generalization ability. Additionally, to compare the classification performance at different thresholds, we calculated the False Positive Rate (FPR), True Positive Rate (TPR), Precision, and Recall at multiple thresholds, and plotted the ROC and PR curves (Fig. 2). It is clearly evident from the figure that CG-AMP outperforms the other comparison models in both the ROC and PR curves on the AMPlify and DAMP benchmark datasets. This result further demonstrates that CG-AMP exhibits higher classification ability and stability in the antimicrobial peptide (AMP) recognition task.

sec.title: Ablation experiments
sec.p: The design of CG-AMP was a key factor in its outstanding performance: the model integrated multiple features to represent sequence information and incorporated contrastive learning and a gated convolutional neural network (GCNN) within its architecture to learn complementary feature representations. To assess the contribution of each component, we conducted a series of ablation experiments, which included the following four variants: (1) CG-AMP-M (pre-trained features module): Removed the multi-dimensional features input and the corresponding GCNN module. (2) CG-AMP-P (multi-dimensional features module): Removed the pre-trained features input and its associated contrastive learning module. (3) CG-AMP-MC: Further removed the contrastive learning module based on CG-AMP-M. (4) CG-AMP-PG: Further removed the GCNN module based on CG-AMP-P. All ablation variants were trained and tested under the same hyperparameter settings and evaluated on two benchmark datasets. The experimental results on the AMPlify dataset (Fig. 3A; Table 6) showed that CG-AMP-M exhibits a performance drop compared to CG-AMP, with accuracy and MCC decreasing by 1.2% and 2.4%, respectively. Furthermore, CG-AMP-P demonstrated an even greater decline in performance compared to CG-AMP-M, with accuracy and MCC decreasing by 1.7% and 3.5%, respectively. These findings not only highlighted the critical roles of both the multi-dimensional features module and the pre-trained features module within the model, but also underscored the superiority of the pre-trained features module. This may have been attributed to the richer information encoded in the ESM-2 features used by the pre-trained module. Moreover, CG-AMP-P outperformed CG-AMP-PG by 12% in accuracy (Acc) and 24% in MCC, while CG-AMP-M showed an improvement of 1% in Acc and 2% in MCC over CG-AMP-MC. These experimental results fully validate the crucial role of the contrastive learning and GCNN modules in extracting effective features. Additionally, the superior performance of CG-AMP-MC compared to CG-AMP-PG further emphasize the key role of pre-trained features in the model. We repeated the above ablation experiments on the DAMP dataset, and the results (Fig. 3B; Table 7) further validated the model’s effectiveness and robustness, corroborating the reliability of the aforementioned conclusions.

To further validate the computational efficiency advantage of GCNN, we compared GCNN and LSTM architectures under the same feature dimensionality and number of layers. The results show that GCNN has an inference time of 0.231 s, a training time of 280.41 s, and 1.38 M parameters, whereas LSTM has an inference time of 0.426 s, a training time of 628.07 s, and 2.74 M parameters. Moreover, GCNN slightly outperforms LSTM in prediction accuracy. These quantitative results demonstrate that in our CGAMP model, the computational efficiency and predictive performance of using GCNN are significantly superior to those of LSTM (Table 8). To ensure a fair comparison between the pre-trained and multi-dimensional feature modules, we further conducted an ablation experiment in which the ESM-2 embeddings were projected to a low-dimensional space comparable to the 45-dimensional multi-dimensional features using principal component analysis (PCA). The results (Table 9) indicate that when feature dimensions are balanced, the performance gap between CG-AMP-M and CG-AMP-P is reduced. Accordingly, the observed advantage of the ESM-2 module primarily reflects the efficiency and informativeness of the pre-trained embeddings.

sec.title: Fusion strategies comparison
sec.p: To optimize the feature fusion strategy for the representations processed by the contrastive learning module and the GCNN module in the CG-AMP model, we systematically compared three different fusion methods after dimensionality reduction (maximum pooling followed by projection to a 64-dimensional space). The experimental process included: (1) Linear Fusion: A weighted combination of embeddings, where weights were learnable parameters. (2) Concatenation Fusion: Direct concatenation of feature vectors at the channel level. (3) Attention-based Fusion: Adaptive feature integration through a multi-head attention mechanism. As shown in Fig. 3C and D, linear fusion exhibited the best performance, while concatenation fusion and attention-based fusion methods showed relatively poorer results. This phenomenon may be attributed to two factors: first, the concatenation method, being overly simplistic, failed to effectively mine feature information, resulting in the underutilization of potential correlations between features. Second, while attention-based fusion theoretically had advantages, its complexity may have led to the over-complication of feature information in this application scenario, thus affecting the overall performance of the model.

sec.title: The feature visualization of CG-AMP
sec.p: To evaluate the effectiveness of the feature representations learned by the CG-AMP model in the AMP recognition task, this study used t-SNE dimensionality reduction for visual analysis of the feature representations. As shown in Fig. 4, the visualized objects included pre-trained features, multi-dimensional features, features extracted by the GCNN module, features enhanced by the contrastive learning module, and the fused features. Experimental results showed that, compared to traditional multi-dimensional features, pre-trained features exhibited more significant inter-class separability, validating the superiority of pre-trained features. Further feature fusion experiments demonstrated that by integrating multi-source complementary information, the model’s discriminative ability was significantly enhanced. Overall, CG-AMP demonstrated its capability to learn effective features representations that could accurately distinguish AMPs from non-AMPs, confirming its efficient feature learning potential for AMP recognition tasks.

sec.title: Comparison with other dual module architecture
sec.p: The dual-module network architecture played a pivotal role in AMP prediction tasks and had a direct impact on model performance. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed dual-module architecture, we designed comparative experiments involving six alternative dual-module configurations. Specifically, we replaced the corresponding components of the original model with widely adopted neural network modules to construct six combinations: CL + BiLSTM25, CL + GCN48, CL + Transformer49, BiLSTM + GCNN, GCN + GCNN, and Transformer + GCNN, where CL denotes the contrastive learning module. It is worth noting that we utilized ESMFold42 to predict the three-dimensional structures of peptide sequences and employed Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) to model and learn the structural information. As shown in Fig. 5, among all configurations, the CL + GCNN architecture consistently outperformed the others across multiple evaluation metrics, thereby demonstrating its superior effectiveness in AMP identification tasks.

sec.title: Assessment of model generalization
sec.p: To further assess the generalization ability of the model, two independent evaluations were conducted. First, considering that ESM-2 was pre-trained on UniProt and that the negative samples in AMPlify also originated from UniProt, there exists a potential risk of data leakage. To mitigate this risk, sequences in the AMPlify and DAMP test sets that overlapped with UniRef50 (the training dataset of ESM-2) were removed, resulting in a clean, independent test set. In the AMPlify test set, 583 overlapping sequences were removed, leaving 1,085 sequences for subsequent evaluation. Re-evaluation on this cleaned test set showed that the model’s performance remained stable and even exhibited a slight improvement (see Supplementary Table S1), indicating that the model maintains robust generalization ability on completely unseen sequences. Second, to further evaluate the model’s performance on truly external data, an independent test set was constructed from the iAMP-bert50 assessment dataset, which had not been used during training or validation. This test set contains 60 randomly selected positive samples (AMPs) and 60 negative samples (non-AMPs), with a maximum sequence length of 100 amino acids—shorter than the maximum length of 183 amino acids in the training set—and notable differences in the lengths and distributions of the amino acid sequences (see Supplementary Fig S1). On this independent test set, our model achieved an accuracy of 0.75, significantly higher than the 0.62 accuracy of the second-best model, TriStack (see Supplementary Table S1). These results indicate that our model possesses stronger discriminative capability in distinguishing positive and negative samples, further confirming its stability and robust generalization performance.

sec.title: Discussion and conclusion
sec.p: This study proposes a novel dual-module feature fusion computational framework, CG-AMP, which combined multi-source sequence features and a dual-module feature extraction strategy for the recognition of AMPs. Specifically, the features we utilized included pre-trained features (ESM-2) and multi-dimensional features, including BLOSUM62, Z-scale, and one-hot encoding. Additionally, the CG-AMP framework consisted of two complementary feature extraction modules: First, to address the potential redundancy in the initial pre-trained features, we introduced an encoder based on a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and trained it using a contrastive learning strategy. Through this approach, the encoder not only effectively learned the features extracted by the ESM-2 pre-trained model but also actively removed redundant information, thereby enhancing its ability to identify key information and improving the discriminative power of the features. Second, to efficiently capture long-range dependencies between sequence features, we employed a GCNN to model the multi-dimensional features extracted from the sequences. By parallelizing convolution operations and incorporating gating mechanisms, GCNN was able to deeply explore the latent global and local information between features, providing richer and more fine-grained representations. In selecting the feature fusion strategy, we evaluated several methods, including simple concatenation, linear fusion, and attention-based fusion. Experimental results indicate that linear fusion outperforms more complex strategies, likely because the features optimized through contrastive learning already exhibit strong discriminative power and complementarity. Although attention-based fusion theoretically enables richer feature interactions, it introduces additional parameters and computational overhead, which may increase the risk of overfitting. Therefore, linear fusion offers an efficient, robust, and interpretable approach for integrating features while preserving their independence and complementarity, demonstrating that when features are sufficiently optimized, a simple fusion strategy can effectively balance predictive performance and model complexity. In summary, the high performance of the CG-AMP model was attributed to two main factors: (1) CG-AMP extracted sequence features from multiple perspectives, encompassing the contextual information, evolutionary data, and physicochemical properties of the peptide sequences; (2) CG-AMP achieved complementary fusion of features through its dual-module architecture, fully leveraging the rich information within the sequences. This enhanced the model’s ability to recognize complex sequence patterns and strengthened its generalization capability. CG-AMP demonstrated significant performance advantages in the AMP prediction task.

However, despite the model’s strong performance, there was still potential for further optimization. For example, some of the initial values and ranges of hyperparameters in this study were derived from previous research and were preliminarily determined under limited experimental conditions. In the future, we can further optimize the parameter configuration through large-scale model training. Additionally, the features extracted using the ESM-2 language model have already positively impacted the model’s performance. To further improve the model, future work could explore integrating features from other pre-trained models, such as ProtT551, to obtain more comprehensive sequence representations. Currently, the model primarily relies on sequence-level information. This is partly because three-dimensional structure prediction of peptides still carries considerable uncertainty, which may introduce errors and affect prediction accuracy. Therefore, using sequence information remains a more robust strategy. However, relying solely on sequence information may limit the model’s ability to capture structural and functional features of peptides. Moreover, the interpretability of the model remains limited, and its generalizability to highly diverse peptide families still requires systematic validation. Future research will proceed along two directions. First, we plan to incorporate secondary and tertiary structural information of peptides52, such as α-helix content, hydrophobic surface area, and contact map features, and generate structural embeddings using high-accuracy structure prediction tools like AlphaFold253, aiming to enhance the model’s ability to represent spatial conformations and identify key functional sites. Second, we aim to fine-tune CG-AMP or apply multi-task learning on datasets of peptides with diverse functions, such as antiviral peptides (AVPs)54 and anticancer peptides (ACPs)55, to systematically assess its cross-task adaptability and transferability. These efforts will lay the foundation for developing a more generalizable and interpretable framework for peptide function prediction.

At the same time, with the rapid development of artificial intelligence technologies, high-precision tools specifically designed for peptide sequence structure prediction may emerge in the future. Utilizing these structural insights is expected to further enhance the model’s performance. As a method focused on AMP recognition, CG-AMP’s flexible architecture gives it broad applicability, and it holds promise for future expansion into other sequence-based biological classification tasks.
